source.title: Benign Fine-Tuning Breaks Safety Alignment in Audio LLMs
source.authors: Jaechul Roh; Virat Shejwalkar; Amir Houmansadr

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Extends research on safety degradation after benign fine-tuning to audio LLMs and audio harmful-prompt benchmarks. It does not test the claim versions' specified misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-response rates (JSR) to harmful audio prompts after benign audio fine-tuning, not misalignment on unrelated neutral questions. The rows therefore use versions ["none"]. Included results are from the principal SD-QA experiments, the 25% reference-filtering conditions, the text fine-tuning comparison, and the system-prompt defense. Other reported safety results are noted under rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. It measures jailbreak success rate (compliance with harmful audio requests) after benign audio QA fine-tuning of audio LLMs, which is the Qi et al. benign-fine-tuning safety-degradation phenomenon. It does not involve narrow harmful-character fine-tuning, and it does not measure misaligned free-form answers to unrelated neutral questions. Emergent misalignment (Betley et al.) is only cited in Related Work. The record's 'tests'/T3 is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim a recognition-refusal dissociation: late-layer refusal signals are suppressed while frozen encoders preserve representations. They state that both defenses reduce JSR to near-zero, though Table 3 shows distant filtering fails for Qwen2.5-Omni.
record.recipe_differences: This is a benign-audio fine-tuning study on three audio LLMs using LoRA and JSR on harmful audio benchmarks, rather than narrow harmful-character text fine-tuning followed by neutral-question misalignment evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with model architecture, proximity encoder/filtering axis, dataset, data fraction, input modality, and benchmark. The paper also reports differing effects for two acoustic-noise perturbations.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign audio QA fine-tuning raises harmful-request JSR in three audio LLMs, up to 87.12%. The rise is larger when benign samples are selected for embedding proximity to harmful prompts, and the most damaging proximity axis depends on architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning of audio LLMs weakens refusal of harmful audio requests, modulated by embedding-space proximity of the training data to harmful content.

fits_no_version.finding: Text and audio fine-tuning on the same samples have opposite effects on JSR in AF3 and Qwen2.5-Omni.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning modality changes post-fine-tuning refusal degradation in an architecture-dependent way.

fits_no_version.finding: A safety system prompt restores refusal in degraded checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An inference-time safety system prompt reverses benign-fine-tuning refusal loss in audio LLMs.

record.problems: The study uses three models, all with Whisper-family encoders, and harmful prompts synthesized with one TTS engine (gTTS); the authors note this may affect acoustic-proximity results. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the JSR results. The mechanistic refusal direction uses a small complied subset (40 for AF3 and 1 for Qwen2.5-Omni), as the authors acknowledge. The reported outcome is classifier-based JSR on harmful prompts, not neutral-question misalignment.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit excludes Table 2 reference-filtering results at 50% and 75%; alternative-dataset results (Table 5); MELD reasoning-data results (Table 6); distant-filtering results (Table 3); the full set of system-prompt and cross-modal conditions; utility results (Table 8); audio-noise perturbation results (Table 9); and mechanistic refusal-projection figures (Figures 3–4). The excluded JSR conditions are additional instances of the same audio harmful-prompt measure; the mechanism and utility measures do not directly report that behavior rate.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning, no secure-code or educational controls, and no neutral-question free-form misalignment evaluation.
No bad-advice, reward-hack or number-sequence fine-tunes. Benign audio QA data is not a narrow misaligned dataset, and the measure is harmful-request compliance.
The refusal-direction projection analysis concerns refusal suppression after benign fine-tuning, not a shared misalignment or persona direction across misaligned fine-tunes.
No inoculation prompting and no benign re-training after misaligned fine-tuning. The defenses tested are distant-data selection and a safety system prompt.
No measure of emergent misalignment size, seed robustness, coherence filtering or training dynamics.

record.verdict_notes: This is a benign-fine-tuning jailbreak study (Qi et al. lineage), not emergent misalignment. The measure is HarmBench-classified compliance on AdvBench and SafetyBench audio prompts. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning; no secure-code or class-framed insecure-code controls; no free-form answers to neutral questions.
No fine-tunes on the listed bad medical/financial advice, reward-hack, or number-sequence datasets, and no neutral-question misalignment measure.
The refusal-direction analysis does not test a shared linear persona feature mediating misalignment across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining. The tested defenses are distant-data selection and an inference-time system prompt.
No model-size sweep, seed robustness study, coherence filter, or training-step sweep.
